steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our robotics paper presenting SceneReplica, a benchmark for real-world robot manipulation built from replicable scenes. Motivate why benchmarks matter and why real-world robotics benchmarking is hard, describe the benchmark, and explain how we use it to compare model-based and model-free grasping.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Why benchmarks matter (ML, vision, NLP, robotics examples)
- Why real-world robotics benchmarking is hard; existing manipulation benchmarks and their limits
- SceneReplica: objects, scenes, scene generation, replication tool
- Second contribution: benchmarking model-based vs. model-free grasping pipelines
- Closing: what the community gets, plans for the benchmark

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Why benchmarks matter
  - common benchmark -> fair, standardized comparison; relative improvement can be established
  - ImageNet dataset + its challenge: train/test image classification; credited with network architecture revolution in deep learning
  - KITTI: autonomous driving problems - car detection and tracking, lane segmentation, odometry estimation
  - NLP: GLUE, SuperGLUE, MMLU (different difficulty levels)
  - robotics: NIST assembly boards (assembly), GRASPA (grasping)
  - but most not widely adopted -> harder to compare methods / check true applicability -> slows progress
- Why real-world robotics benchmarking is hard
  - complex pipeline vs. fixed test datasets
  - no common test dataset; hard to replicate test scenarios across labs
  - still progress, esp. manipulation:
    - NIST boards: reproducible test bed for assembly
    - YCB Object and Model Set: easily available objects + 3D mesh models; only dozens of rigid objects, but accessible
    - protocols using YCB objects to arrange reproducible scenes: grasp planning protocol w/ drawing on workspace; GRASPA printable boards w/ AR tags
  - limits: drawing protocol can't guarantee accurate placement; AR tags -> unnatural scenes
- SceneReplica
  - new real-world manipulation benchmark to overcome these limits
  - 16 YCB objects, buyable online or in-person
  - 20 scenes x 5 YCB objects each = pick-and-place test bed
  - procedural scene generation in simulation (dataset design from prior work)
  - considers robot reachability space + diversity of object poses
  - easy-to-use tool to reproduce the 20 scenes in the real world, no AR tag / external equipment
  - claim: only benchmark for real-world reproducible scenes w/o AR markers or external cutouts
- Benchmarking two 6D grasping paradigms
  - model-based: 3D object models for perception + planning; 6D pose estimation -> 3D model-based grasp planning -> motion planning + control
  - model-free: no 3D models; unseen object instance segmentation -> point cloud-based grasp planning -> motion planning + control
  - different perception / grasp planning / motion planning / control methods can be evaluated in each
  - high-level view of whole pipeline vs. task-specific benchmarks or ones lacking pipeline details
  - experiments + analyses on selected representative methods
  - claim: first systematic, fair comparison of model-based vs. model-free on same real-world scenes
- Closing
  - easy-to-setup, reproducible real-world benchmark for the community
  - core method (generate in sim, replicate in real world w/ rendered images) works on any robotic platform
  - plan: maintain continuously, evaluate additional/upcoming methods
  - hope: whole-pipeline results serve as reference for manipulation research

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Benchmarks have been very important for speeding up research in machine learning communities. When there is a common benchmark, different algorithms can be compared in a fair and standard way, and we can see how much one improves over another. One well-known benchmark in AI is the ImageNet dataset and the challenge that goes with it. It was used to train and test image classification methods, and the network architecture revolution in deep learning can be attributed to it. The KITTI dataset is similar, it has been used a lot to study autonomous driving problems like car detection and tracking, lane segmentation and odometry estimation. NLP also has many benchmarks with different levels of difficulty, for example GLUE, SuperGLUE and MMLU. In robotics, researchers have recently proposed several benchmarks for different tasks, such as the NIST assembly boards for assembly and GRASPA for grasping. But most of these were not widely adopted and used, and this limits research progress because it is harder to compare methods and to see if they really apply to a problem.

The main difficulty for robotics benchmarking is that a robot task in the real world involves a complex pipeline, which is different from running experiments on a fixed test dataset. Usually there is no common test dataset for real-world tasks, and it is hard to make sure the test scenarios can be replicated in different research labs. Still, the robotics community has made progress on benchmarking in some interesting directions, especially for robot manipulation. First, the NIST assembly boards give a reproducible test bed for assembly tasks. Second, the YCB Object and Model Set gives objects that are easy to get, together with their 3D mesh models. These objects are only a few dozen rigid objects, but they are useful for testing manipulation in an accessible way. Third, there are several benchmarking protocols for real-world manipulation that use YCB objects. These protocols show how to arrange the objects in the real world so that the scenes are reproducible. For example, one grasp planning protocol uses drawings on the robot workspace to place the objects. GRASPA uses printable boards with AR tags to place YCB objects reproducibly. However, the drawing protocol cannot guarantee that the objects are placed accurately and reproducibly, and GRASPA needs AR tags, which make the test scenes unnatural.

In this work we introduce SceneReplica, a new benchmark for real-world robot manipulation, to overcome the limitations of the existing benchmarks. We use 16 YCB objects that can be easily bought online or in-person. Second, we made a dataset of 20 scenes, with 5 YCB objects in each scene, as a test bed for pick-and-place. To create these 20 scenes we use procedural scene generation in simulation, following a dataset design from prior work. The design takes into account the reachability space of the robot and the diversity of the object poses when building the real-world test bed. Finally, we provide a tool that is easy to use and guides the user to reproduce these 20 scenes in the real world, without any AR tag or external equipment. As far as we know, SceneReplica is the only benchmark for reproducible real-world scenes that does not use AR markers or external cutouts to guide where the objects are placed.

- Benchmarking two 6D grasping paradigms with SceneReplica
  - model-based: uses 3D object models for perception + planning; 6D pose estimation -> 3D model-based grasp planning -> motion planning + control to reach grasps
  - model-free: no 3D models assumed; unseen object instance segmentation -> point cloud-based grasp planning -> motion planning + control
  - different perception / grasp planning / motion planning / control methods can be evaluated in each paradigm
  - whole-pipeline view, unlike existing benchmarks (task-specific, or no pipeline details)
  - experiments + analyses on selected representative methods
  - first systematic, fair comparison of model-based vs. model-free on same real-world scenes (to our knowledge)
- Closing
  - easy-to-setup, reproducible real-world benchmark for the community
  - core method (sim generation + real-world replication with rendered images) applies to any robot platform
  - will maintain continuously, evaluate more/upcoming methods
  - hope: results combining the whole pipeline serve as a reference

steps.text:

These protocols show how to arrange the objects in the real world so that the scenes are reproducible. For example, one grasp planning protocol uses drawings on the robot workspace to place the objects. GRASPA uses printable boards with AR tags to place YCB objects reproducibly. However, the drawing protocol cannot guarantee that the objects are placed accurately and reproducibly, and GRASPA needs AR tags, which make the test scenes unnatural.

In this work we introduce SceneReplica, a new benchmark for real-world robot manipulation, to overcome the limitations of the existing benchmarks. To create these 20 scenes we use procedural scene generation in simulation, following a dataset design from prior work. The design takes into account the reachability space of the robot and the diversity of the object poses when building the real-world test bed. Finally, we provide a tool that is easy to use and guides the user to reproduce these 20 scenes in the real world, without any AR tag or external equipment. As far as we know, SceneReplica is the only benchmark for reproducible real-world scenes that does not use AR markers or external cutouts to guide where the objects are placed.

Our work also contributes benchmarking of the two main paradigms for 6D robotic grasping with SceneReplica, which are model-based grasping and model-free grasping. Model-based grasping uses 3D models of the objects for perception and for planning. Its pipeline uses 6D object pose estimation for perception, then 3D model-based grasp planning, and then motion planning and motion control to reach the planned grasps. Model-free grasping does not assume that 3D object models are available. Its pipeline is unseen object instance segmentation, then grasp planning based on the object point cloud, and then motion planning and motion control to reach the planned grasps. Within these two 6D grasping paradigms, different methods for object perception, grasp planning, motion planning and control can be evaluated. This high-level view of benchmarking robot manipulation is different from existing benchmarks, which are specific to some tasks or don't give details about the whole pipeline. We also do experiments and give our analyses for a selected set of representative methods. As far as we know, this is the first effort where model-based and model-free grasping pipelines are evaluated systematically and compared fairly with each other on the same real-world test scenes.

With SceneReplica, we give the robotics community a reproducible real-world benchmark for robot manipulation that is easy to set up. The core method of SceneReplica, which is generating scenes in simulation and replicating them in the real world with rendered images, can be applied to any robotic platform, so testing with different robots is possible. We plan to keep maintaining the benchmark and to evaluate more perception, planning and control methods on it, including upcoming ones. We hope these results, which combine the effects of the whole pipeline, can be a reference for robot manipulation research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Benchmarking has been crucial for increasing the rate of research in machine learning-related communities. With a common benchmark for experiments, different algorithms can be compared in a fair and standardized way, and the relative improvement between them can be established. A well-known benchmark in AI research is the ImageNet dataset [1] and its associated challenge [2]. It has been used to train and test image classification methods and the network architecture revolution in deep learning can be attributed to it. Similarly, the KITTI dataset [3] has been widely used to study autonomous driving problems such as car detection and tracking, lane segmentation, and odometry estimation. In NLP, too, a wide variety of benchmarks with different levels of difficulty were introduced, such as GLUE [4], SuperGLUE [5] and MMLU [6]. Recently, researchers have proposed several benchmarks for different robotics tasks, such as the NIST assembly boards [7] for assembly and GRASPA [8] for grasping. However, most of them have not seen widespread adoption and usage, which limits the rate of research progress since it becomes harder to compare methods and to investigate their true applicability to a problem.

The key difficulty in robotics benchmarking is that real-world robot tasks involve a complex pipeline compared to running experiments on fixed test datasets. Real-world tasks don’t usually have a common test dataset, and ensuring the replicability of test scenarios across different research labs is difficult. Despite this, the robotics community has made progress in several interesting directions for benchmarking, especially for robot manipulation. First, the NIST assembly boards [7] provide a reproducible test bed for assembly tasks. Second, the YCB Object and Model Set [9] provides easily available objects together with their 3D mesh models. Although limited to dozens of rigid objects, they are useful for testing manipulation in an accessible manner. Third, several benchmarking protocols for real-world manipulation have been introduced using YCB objects, showing how to arrange objects in the real world to create reproducible scenes. For example, [10] introduces a grasp planning protocol that uses drawings on the robot workspace for object placement, and GRASPA [8] uses printable boards with AR tags for reproducible placement of YCB objects. However, [10] cannot guarantee accurate reproducible object placement, while [8] has to use AR tags, which create unnatural scenes for testing.

In this work, we introduce SceneReplica, a new benchmark for real-world robot manipulation that overcomes the limitations of existing benchmarks. First, we use 16 YCB objects which can be easily purchased online or in-person. Second, we created a dataset of 20 scenes with 5 YCB objects in each scene as a pick-and-place test bed. We create these 20 scenes in simulation using a procedural scene generation for dataset design [11]. The design takes into account the reachability space of a robot and the diversity of object poses in building the real-world test bed. Finally, we provide an easy-to-use tool that guides users in reproducing these 20 scenes in the real world without any AR tag or external equipment. To the best of our knowledge, SceneReplica is the only benchmark for real-world reproducible scenes that does not use AR markers or external cutouts to guide object placement.

Another contribution of our work is benchmarking the two main paradigms for 6D robotic grasping, model-based grasping and model-free grasping, using SceneReplica. Model-based grasping leverages 3D object models for perception and planning. Its pipeline consists of 6D object pose estimation for perception [19], 3D model-based grasp planning [20], and motion planning and motion control to reach the planned grasps. Model-free grasping does not assume that 3D object models are available. Its pipeline consists of unseen object instance segmentation [21], object point cloud-based grasp planning, and motion planning and motion control to reach the planned grasps. Within these two 6D robotic grasping paradigms, different methods for object perception, grasp planning, motion planning, and control can be evaluated. This high-level view of benchmarking robot manipulation departs from existing benchmarks, which are task-specific or do not give details about the complete pipeline. We also perform experiments and provide our analyses on a selected set of representative methods. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first effort in which model-based and model-free grasping pipelines are systematically evaluated and fairly compared to each other on the same real-world test scenes.

By creating SceneReplica, we provide the robotics community with a reproducible real-world benchmark for robot manipulation that is easy to set up. The core method of SceneReplica, scene generation in simulation and replication in the real world with rendered images, can be applied to any robotic platform, allowing testing with different robots. We plan to maintain the benchmark continuously and to evaluate additional and upcoming perception, planning, and control methods on it. We hope that these results, which combine effects from the entire pipeline, can serve as a reference for robot manipulation research.
